(I)
QUESTION PRESENTED
The Court granted review of  the following question
presented*:
Whether the First Amendment’s established chillingeffect doctrine—under which a credible government
threat that deters the exercise of fundamental rights constitutes a complete and independently actionable
constitutional injury—is displaced by Williamson
County’s land-use finality requirement when a plaintiff alleges that government threat s both before and after a
Planning Commission meeting chilled religious exercise,
worship, and assembly.

 
* In his opening brief, petitioner alters the question presented.  Br. i;
see infra pp.24, 54.

II

and Luke McConville, former City Law Director, in his individual capacity, † were Appellees in the U.S. Court of

District Court for the Northern District of Ohio below.

Siemborski.  C.A. Appellant Br. 2 n.1.

CITY OF UNIVERSITY HEIGHTS, OHIO, ET AL.,

ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE SIXTH CIRCUIT



BRIEF FOR RESPONDENTS


STATEMENT
Respondent City of Univer sity Heights respects the
right of its citizens to pray in  their homes.  The City also
welcomes the establishment of formal houses of religious
assembly.  The City’s zoning code recognizes houses of assembly as among the “most desirable use[s] of the land in
the City.”  UHCO § 1274.01(a), Pet.App.74a.  Accordingly,
the Code authorizes the City’s Planning Commission to

2

grant special-use permits to establish houses of assembly
in residential areas.
This case is not about whether petitioner Daniel
Grand can host small prayer groups in his home.  When
petitioner lived in University Heights (until he moved in
July 2026), no provision of Ci ty law barred small prayer
groups.  The zoning authorit ies never told him he could
not host small prayer groups  without a permit, and the
City expressly reaffirmed in the district-court proceedings that he could.
The case arises from a seri es of events triggered by
petitioner’s January 2021 invitation announcing the inauguration of a “Beis Hakenes et” (Hebrew for “House of
Assembly”) in his home.  That invitation prompted concerns about application of th e City’s zoning laws, which
require special-use permits for “houses of assembly” in
residential districts.  As th e permitting process played
out, petitioner clarified that he did not intend to establish
a house of assembly and instead wished only to host a
small prayer group.  But before the City could decide that
he did not need a permit, he withdrew his application and
terminated the process.  He nevertheless sued to challenge the City’s zoning law eighteen months later.
That challenge is moot.  Petitioner sold his home, no
longer lives in University Heights, and is no longer subject
to the challenged ordinance.  Even before he moved, respondents affirmed in the district-court proceedings that
there was no ongoing controversy:  the City’s laws do not
require a special-use permit to  host small prayer groups
in one’s home.  Pet.App.38a-39a.
To avoid mootness, petitioner now claims to be pursuing claims for damages or retrospective relief.  But

3

petitioner affirmatively moved for entry of summary judgment in the district court an d did not say anything about
seeking damages.  Nor did he say he was pursuing damages in the Sixth Circuit—even after respondents argued
mootness.  Rather, the Sixth Circuit understood petitioner
to assert a preenforcement challenge to the ordinance’s
application.  Petitioner cannot obtain relief from an ordinance that no longer applies to him or his property.
In all events, the federal courts lacked jurisdiction
over petitioner’s challenge to the ordinance from the outset.  The district court and the Sixth Circuit—in a
unanimous decision by then-Chief Judge Sutton—correctly dismissed petitioner’s  claims as unripe under
Williamson County Regional  Planning Commission v.
Hamilton Bank of Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172 (1985).
Williamson County recognizes that when it comes to
application of discretionary zo ning laws like this one,
courts ordinarily cannot determine whether a law “inflicts
an actual, concrete injury”—i.e., whether the plaintiff has
suffered Article III injury—until  zoning authorities have
applied the law to the plaintiff’s intended land use.  Id. at
193.  Petitioner’s summary-judgment and appellate briefs
described his claims as cha llenging application of the
City’s special-use permit ordi nance to his desired prayer
groups.  But the Planning Commission had not determined that the ordinance applied.  The Sixth Circuit
correctly concluded that p etitioner’s as-applied “challenges to the ordinance are unripe” because he “withdrew
his application for a special use permit before anyone had
a chance to adopt an interpr etation of the ordinance or
even to determine whether Grand needed a special use
permit in the first place.”  Pet.App.8a-9a.

4

To be sure, Williamson County does not apply to
every religious-liberty claim in the land-use context.  For
example, as the Sixth Circuit observed, it does not govern
ripeness of facial challenges to zoning laws.  Pet.App.14a.
Petitioner abandoned a facial challenge below.
Pet.App.14a.  To the extent petitioner now attempts to assert other claims—for example, that the City
discriminated against him by  refusing to collect his
trash—he abandoned those claims as well.  The Sixth Circuit reasonably understood p etitioner to be asserting a
preenforcement, as-applied challenge to the ordinance
and correctly applied Williamson County  to hold that
challenge unripe.
The Court should either affirm or dismiss the petition. 
A. Factual Background
1.  University Heights is a Cleveland suburb with a
population of about 14,000.  About 20-25% of the City’s
population is Orthodox Jewish.1
The Cleveland area does not have a perfect record
when it comes to welcoming Orthodox Jews.  University
Heights has tried to improve its record.  In 2023, the City
amended its charter to prohibit discrimination by the City
on the basis of religion, among other grounds.  University
Heights Charter art. 8, § 12.  In 2025, the City adopted a
resolution, introduced by respondent and former-Mayor
Michael Brennan, expressing  the City’s “commitment to
keep members of the City’s Jewish community safe from
expressions of hate and physical harm.”  Res. No. 2025-31
(University Heights 2025), https://perma.cc/XWT4-
 
1 Grace Gilson, Michele Weiss and Justin Brasch Mark Milestones as
First Orthodox Jewish Mayors in Their Cities , Jewish Telegraphic
Agency (Jan. 2, 2026), https://perma.cc/46TJ-FTEY.

5

YD6B.  Also in 2025, the City’s voters elected as mayor
Michele Weiss, a longtime councilmember and Vice
Mayor.  Weiss is reportedly the first practicing Orthodox
Jewish woman to be elected mayor in the Nation. 2  Weiss
is a respondent in these proceedings in her official capacity.
Recently, the City’s growing Orthodox population has
outpaced its existing religiou s infrastructure.  Some City
residents have responded by opening “shuls” in buildings
zoned for residential purposes .  The word “shul” in Yiddish typically means “synagogue,” 3 and the Jewish
community regularly uses “shu l” to refer to synagogues,
including in the University Heights area.4
Several home shuls in the City have functioned as traditional synagogues, operated by boards and generally
open to members of the commu nity.  One home shul featured a sanctuary, children’s classroom, nursery, kitchen,
offices, and a social hall.5  Another home shul once hosted
120 to 130 worshippers in the basement.  D. Ct. Dkt. 83-1
at 55 (Brennan Dep.).   And, on another occasion, a house
was purchased specifically for hosting religious services.
Id. at 58.
 
2 Gilson, supra, n.1.
3 Shul, American Heritage Dictionar y of the English Language (5th
ed. 2018).
4 See, e.g. , Congregation Zichron Chaim, About Us ,
https://perma.cc/9QVC-DA33 (“Congregation Zichron Chaim … is an
orthodox synagogue.  … The roots of our shul date back to 1975.”);
Khal Yereim, https://perma.cc/6TSW-6KBU  (synagogue describing
itself as a “full-service shul serving the Cleveland Heights community”).
5 Abigail Preiszig, University Heights OKs Special-Use Permit for
Synagogue on University Parkway , Cleveland Jewish News (Mar.
21, 2025), https://perma.cc/PB4K-YMZD.

6

Many of these home shuls were originally created
without permits allowing them  to operate as houses of
worship in residential areas.6  Id. at 36, 94.  In University
Heights, as in many cities, residential zoning districts are
designed only to contain resi dential structures.  University Heights’ U-1 residential districts permit only singlefamily dwellings, buildings owned by a board of education
or municipality (like public schools), and libraries.  UHCO
§ 1250.02, Pet.App.71a.
The general provisions governing U-1 residential districts, however, are just the de fault rules.  The Code also
allows property uses within U-1 districts that “foster the
most desirable use of the land in the City,” identified in a
Code section titled “Houses of Assembly and Social Service Uses.”  Id. § 1274.01(a), Pet.App.74a.  The City’s
Planning Commission must approve special-use permits
for these uses, which include “[ h]ouses of worship or religious education, including churches, temples, synagogues,
religious organizations, pa rish houses and parochial
schools.”  Id. § 1274.01(b)(1), Pet.App.74a.  The permit requirement ensures that the special use does not “impair
surrounding property values or uses, vehicular parking
and pedestrian or traffic conditions,” and is not “otherwise
contrary to the public heal th, safety and welfare.”  Id.
§ 1274.01(d), Pet.App.75a-76a.
Special uses are subject to additional rules like structure height requirements.  But applicants can obtain
variances from those requirements from the Planning
Commission.  Once the Commi ssion approves special-use
permits and variances, the City Council must also sign off.
 
6 Jimmy Oswald, University Heights Approves Permit for Home
Shul, Cleveland Jewish News (June 17, 2026),
https://perma.cc/VF8N-5SG9.

7

Id. §§ 1274.01(a), 1274.02(f)(5), Pet.App.74a, 83a.  The record contains no evidence that the City Council or
Commission has ever denied an application for a specialuse permit for a house of assembly.
The Planning Commission and City Council granted
the Aleksander Shul—the home shul that had hosted 120-
plus worshippers, D. Ct. Dkt. 83-1  at 55—a special-use
permit and the ten variances it needed to operate a synagogue in a house. 7  The City Council also unanimously
approved the Planning Commission’s recommendation of
a special-use permit and five variances to another home
shul, Zichron Asher Zelig, to provide daily services for up
to 150 worshippers.8  The Heichal Hakadosh Synagogue—
the home shul that submitted plans for a sanctuary, social
hall, and offices—also received the permits and variances
it needed to operate in a residential district.9  And the City
authorized the Congregation Zichron Chaim synagogue to
demolish six homes and build a new synagogue in a residential area.10
2.  On January 19, 2021, petitioner Daniel Grand
emailed friends announcing “the inauguration of the
Shomayah Tefillah Beis Hakeneset located at 2343
Miramar Blvd. (The Daniel J. Grand Residence).”
J.A.344.  As petitioner admitted below, the Hebrew phrase
 
7 Jane Kaufman, Council OKs Permit, Variances for Aleksander Shul
to Operate as Synagogue , Cleveland Jewish News (Dec. 7, 2021),
https://perma.cc/3X9M-7ME5.
8 Oswald, supra, n.6.
9 Preiszig, supra, n.5.
10 Jane Kaufman, University Heights Signs Development Agreement
for Zichron Chaim , Cleveland Jewish News (Oct. 20, 2021),
https://perma.cc/KQ42-GKX8.

8

“Beis Hakeneset” means “House of Assembly.”  C.A. Appellant Br. 2. 11  The invitation introduced “our Rabbi—
Rabbi Rosskam” and directed recipients to “the shul entrance.”  J.A.344.  The invitati on also urged recipients to
“spread the word to whomever  you feel might be interested in coming” and “bring someone with you.”  J.A.344-
345.  Petitioner’s attorney later admitted “that [petitioner]
publicly phrased his contemplated use more loftily than he
actually imagined his use would be.”  J.A.295.
Word about petitioner’s shul spread.  Ben Feldman, a
City resident and member of  a local synagogue, became
concerned that someone was “opening a synagogue in
their house on Miramar.”  J. A.193.  On January 21, Feldman sent a Facebook message  to then-Mayor Brennan
with the invitation’s text, noted “a number of these pop up
synagogues in the neighbor hood,” questioned whether
they were adhering to “Covid protocols,” and asked if
Brennan could “put a stop to this.”  J.A.193-194.
Brennan reviewed the invitation and (as he later explained) interpreted it as Feldman did:  the invitation was
“consistent with the formal opening of a synagogue with a
name.”  D. Ct. Dkt. 83-1 at 85.  Brennan testified in a deposition that he wanted to clar ify that use of a home as a
synagogue in a residential area required a permit.  Id.; see
UHCO § 1274.01, Pet.App.74a.  Later that day, Brennan
tried to reach petitioner to clear up “whatever … misunderstanding” existed about whether a house of worship
could be opened without a special-use permit.  D. Ct. Dkt.
83-1 at 73; see also J.A.322.
 
11 Petitioner registered the name Shomayah Tefillah as a not-forprofit organization sometime earlier in New York.  J.A.187; D. Ct.
Dkt. 83-1 at 79.

9

Petitioner did not answer Brennan’s call, J.A.197, so
that same day, January 21, then-City Law Director Luke
McConville emailed petitioner a letter.  The letter explained that petitioner’s home was “zoned U-1 for
residential use” and that “use or operation of the Premises
as a religious place of assemb ly and/or in operation as a
shul or synagogue is not permitted” without a special-use
permit.  J.A.199.  The letter advised that, “[t]o the extent”
petitioner’s home was “currently being used for said purposes or [is] intended to be us ed for such purposes in the
immediate or near future,” petitioner should “immediately
cease and desist any and all su ch operations.”  J.A.199.
The letter stated th at violations “may result in building
code citations” and noted the option to apply for a specialuse permit.  J.A.199-200.
Petitioner and Brennan then spoke by phone, also on
January 21.  In his deposition , petitioner said he thought
Brennan told him that he needed a permit to gather ten
men to pray in his home, alth ough he “c[ould] only paraphrase” and “c[ouldn]’t spea k for” the Mayor.  J.A.152-
154.
Petitioner shared with Brennan that day a copy of the
invitation, but that version di ffered from the original one
that Feldman forwarded to Brennan.  The version from
Feldman referred to the intended gathering as a “shul”
and encouraged recipients to spread the word and invite
others.  J.A.194-195.  The invitation petitioner shared with
Brennan, however, replaced “shul” with “prayer session”
and omitted statements about the rabbi, spreading the
word, and bringing additional guests.  J.A.190-192.
3.  On January 22, 2021, pe titioner applied for a special-use permit.  J.A.201.  The City scheduled petitioner’s
application for a virtual Zoom  hearing before the fivemember Planning Commission on March 4, 2021.  D. Ct.

10

Dkt. 81-9.  Mayor Brennan was one of the five members.
University Heights Charter art. 7, § 2.
Before the hearing, petitioner acknowledged the confusion his invitation had crea ted.  In a March 2 letter to
neighbors, petitioner stated that he did not intend to open
a “‘synagogue’ or ‘shul’ (same word in Yiddish).”  J.A.287.
He explained that “[a] bonafide shul is a community facility that is always open to the public” and that his home, by
contrast, would not be open to  the public.  J.A.288.  He
emphasized:  “We have no desire to operate a bonafide
Synagogue (English) Shul (in Yiddish) or Beit Hakeneset
(Hebrew) out of our home.”  J.A.290.
At the March 4 hearing, the City’s Law Director advised petitioner that he could present evidence supporting
his application and that anyone testifying would be sworn
in and could be cross-examin ed.  J.A.226, 262.  Although
petitioner (at 32) claims the Planning Commission employed an “unprecedented quas i-judicial format,” it used
that format here due to a “quirk[]” in the City’s zoning
code, as the Law Director explained at the hearing.
J.A.225-226, 262.  Applications for special-use permits under Chapter 1274 are deviations  from the zoning code.
Most other matters before the Planning Commission involve applications for property  uses consistent with the
zoning code.  See, e.g., UHCO §§ 1264.01(b), 1280.07(a) &
08(a).  Applications that deviate from the zoning code,
meanwhile, generally fall under the purview of the Board
of Zoning Appeals.  Accordin gly, on the occasions when
the Planning Commission fulfills this typical Zoning
Board function, it uses the quasi-judicial procedures employed by the Board of Zo ning Appeals under Chapter
2506 of the Ohio Revised Code.  J.A.262.  While the procedures in Chapter 2506 are not strictly required by Ohio

11

law, “they are strongly recommended” to avoid “‘infring[ing] on a party’s right to a fair hearing.’”  Michael R.
Moran, Ohio Admin. Law Handbook & Agency Directory
§ 7:6 (2025-26 ed.).
Petitioner appeared with counsel12 at the hearing, and
petitioner and Rabbi Rosska mm testified.  J.A.231-232.
Petitioner’s counsel explained that “this hearing is about
whether a residence of University Heights may host
prayer services in a designated, modest space” that would
be “respectful of and unintrusive upon” neighbors, and described a men’s prayer group meeting once a week and on
certain high holidays .  J.A.232.  Petition er’s counsel also
stated that petitioner was “n ot disputing that [Section
1274.01(b)] applies” to his “Shabbos Shul.”  J.A.232-233.
Residents testified for and against the application.
One neighbor testified that he was “initially concerned
that [petitioner] was going to try and turn [his] house into
a synagogue” but now favored granting the permit because petitioner had “assured [him] that’s not going to be
the case.”  D. Ct. Dkt. 81-11 at 70-71.
Neighbors opposing the permit raised concerns about
traffic, parking, and the freque ncy of the property’s use.
J.A.248-257.  Other neighbors went further.  One resident
suggested that petitioner’s shul was an attempt to obtain
a tax exemption, J.A.247, and another stated that if petitioner wanted to “avoid a walk to [his] existing temple” he
“should have picked somewhere else” to live, J.A.253.  Still
another wrote that she did “not want our neighborhood labeled as Jewish.”  J.A.280.
 
12 According to petitioner, a City representative (possibly now-Mayor
Weiss) had told him by phone to hire an attorney.  D. Ct. Dkt. 80 at
267-268 (Grand Dep.).

12

Hours into the Zoom hearing, the five-member Commission discussed whether to grant, deny, or table the
application for more discussi on.  It was after 10:00 p.m.,
and members of the public repeatedly interrupted the
Commission’s attempts to deliberate.  J.A.260, 264-269.
Commissioner Michael Fine moved to table the application until the next hearing.  He stated that because he
was unsure how the property would be used, petitioner
should “c[o]me back with a more specific request as to
what he wanted.”  J.A.264, 266.  Commissioner April Urban seconded the motion, observing that “there was a
noticeable difference from what [she] heard was the intended use” (i.e., a small prayer group) and what residents
were concerned about (i.e., a synagogue).  J.A.267-268.
The Commission voted 3-2 to table the application for
further discussion at the next public hearing.  J.A.269-270.
Commissioners Siemborski and Brennan opposed tabling.
J.A.269.  Brennan later explained that he voted “no” because he thought the Commission should deliberate
without delay, so that it could “have told Mr. Grand, …
here are some items we would like to have, that would help
us make our decision.”  D. Ct. Dkt. 83-1 at 212.
The day after the hearing, the commissioners corresponded by email with each  other about petitioner’s
application.  See J.A.275-284.  Multiple commissioners expressed discomfort about the “[p]roblematic … rhetoric”
of some members of the public.  J.A.275-284.
On the merits of petition er’s application, Commissioner Fine wrote that he found petitioner’s proposal “not
clear.”  J.A.281.  He “d[id]  not know why anyone would
need a special use permit to invite[] 10 friends to pray with
them,” or “how this would be different th[a]n my having
friends over regularly for part ies.”  J.A.282.  In the same

13

email chain, Commissioner Urban recommended dismissing the application because “the use presented (the
applicant proposed gath[er]ing 10-15 friends at his house
once a week, as well as three times a year on the high holidays, for prayer) does not re quire a special use permit.”
J.A.277.  She asked if it could “be made clear that private
gatherings in one’s home are permissible, but if they occur
at a frequency or size that is  disruptive to the neighbors,
more akin to a house of assembly than a private residence,
actions would need to be taken.”  J.A.278.
Before the Commission cou ld discuss the application
further by email, Law Direct or McConville reminded the
commissioners that deliberation had to occur at a publicly
noticed hearing, as the Mayor explained at the next hearing.  J.A.337.  The Commissi on thus postponed further
discussion until the next hearing.  J.A.337.
On March 16, a week before the next scheduled hearing on March 23, petitioner emailed the Commission to ask
what additional information he should provide.  J.A.296-
297.  Because the commission ers had ceased email communications, they had not yet settled on what materials
they wanted to receive, although one commissioner responded by asking for floorplans and a site plan so that the
Commission could “ensure” the space is “safe for the inhabitants.”  J.A.296.
The next morning, Mayor Brennan responded that
“[t]he Planning Commission  may discuss whether additional materials are needed to make the decision on the
merits,” and that “[i]f such materials are deemed necessary, [petitioner] will be given sufficient time to provide
them.”  J.A.294.
On March 23, an hour before the next hearing, petitioner emailed the Commission to withdraw his

14

application for a special-use permit because he “d[id] not
wish to operate a house of worship as is defined under the
zoning ordinance in the privac y of [his] home.”  J.A.138.
At that time, petitioner unders tood that he “did not need
to seek a permit for a small prayer group.”  Pet. Br. 15.
Petitioner’s opening brief in this Court states that he
withdrew his application because Chapter 1274 prohibits
“sleeping or residential use accommodations” as part of
special-use permits.  P et. Br. 15 (quoting UHCO
§ 1274.02(f)(4), Pet.App.83a).  The Code’s prohibition on
“sleeping or residential use accommodations” is, however,
qualified by the language “[e]xcept for existing approved
uses,” which may have covered petitioner’s existing use of
his home to sleep.  UHCO § 1274.02(f), Pet.App.82a.  In
any event, petitioner never raised that concern when withdrawing his application.  J.A.138.  And because petitioner
withdrew his application, the Commission never addressed whether sleeping in a house of worship was
permitted or whether to gran t a variance to allow such
use.
The Commission met as scheduled on March 23.
Brennan read petitioner’s withdrawal into the record and
reminded attendees that “co ngregating at 2343 Miramar
Boulevard or any other address located in a residence
zoned U-1 without a special-use permit is a violation of city
law.”  J.A.337-338.  He contin ued, “I’m hopeful that the
wording of the withdrawal is not intended to suggest that
congregating weekly at a resi dence to conduct activities
consistent with those in a house of assembly  does not require a special-use permit” and clarified that “there is no
permission granted here to operate a house of assembly or
conduct activities consisten t with one at 2343 Miramar
Boulevard.”  J.A.338-339 (emp hases added).  Brennan
added, “[i]f you observe such activities, and I hope you do

15

not, but if you do, you may report them to the city, and the
city will enforce its laws, which exist for the benefit of the
entire community.”  J.A.339.
The following year, on Fe bruary 18, 2022, the City
sent petitioner a letter prop osing a memorandum of understanding confirming that regular private prayer
gatherings limited to invited guests did not require a special-use permit.  D. Ct. Dkt. 79-1 at 151-153.  The
memorandum would preserve ordinary enforcement of
neutral parking, noise, and other property rules.  Id.  The
record contains no response from petitioner.
4.  In 2021, both before and after petitioner withdrew
his application, his next-door neighbors Jeff and Vivienne
Porter lodged complaints with the City concerning parking, his property’s conditio n, and possible building-code

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
I.  The Court need not decide whether this moot case
was once ripe.  This Court may affirm or dismiss the petition without reaching ripe ness because petitioner’s
challenges to UHCO § 1274 ar e moot.  The Sixth Circuit
understood petitioner to bring preenforcement challenges
to the City’s zoning ordinanc e, seeking prospective relief
to allow him to host prayer groups in his home.  Those
challenges became moot early in the litigation when all
parties agreed that UHCO § 1274 does not require a special-use permit for small prayer groups.  Subsequent
events have only underscored petitioner’s mootness problem.  Mayor Brennan left office last year, mooting any
claim premised on fear that  Brennan would enforce the
ordinance against him.  And then petitioner sold his home
and left University Heights, eliminating any possibility of
enforcement.  Petitioner cannot avoid mootness by belatedly reframing this case as a damages lawsuit.
II.  If the Court addresses ripeness, it should affirm
the Sixth Circuit’s conclusion that the district court lacked
Article III jurisdiction to decide whether UHCO § 1274
was unlawfully applied to petitioner’s property.  The Sixth
Circuit correctly held that petitioner’s as-applied land-use
claims are unripe under the finality requirement  adopted
in Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v.
Hamilton Bank of Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172 (1985).
A.  The finality requirement governs ripeness for
claims challenging land-use re gulations.  Like standing,
ripeness prevents federal courts from adjudicating hypothetical or abstract disputes.  Because of the flexibility

26

built into land-use regulations, a court ordinarily cannot
know from the face of a regula tion what uses of property
will be permitted.  The finality requirement accordingly
recognizes that land-use disputes will not be ripe for adjudication until the “permissibl e uses of the property are
known to a reasonable degree of certainty.”  Palazzolo v.
Rhode Island, 533 U.S. 606, 620 (2001).  Finality is typically satisfied by a decision from local authorities applying
a regulation to the at-issue pr operty, but claims also may
be ripe when a plaintiff can show that local authorities
have reached a de facto final position, such that proceedings before the relevant authorities would be futile.
B.  The finality requirement has always been an Article III rule.  Williamson County  explained—and other
cases confirm—that the finality requirement ensures that
the challenged regulations have caused the plaintiff an actual, concrete injury.  In the preenforcement context,
Williamson County implements Article III’s requirement
that plaintiffs show a credible  threat of enforcement.  No
credible threat— i.e., no concrete injury—exists until
plaintiffs can show that their proposed use is “arguably
proscribed” by the land-use regulation and “the threat of
future enforcement … is substantial.”  Susan B. Anthony
List (SBA) v. Driehaus , 573 U.S. 149, 161-64 (2014).  In
other words, courts lack jurisdiction until it is reasonably
clear how a land-use regulation applies to a proposed use
of property, which is all Williamson County requires.
No principled reason exists to confine this Article III
rule to takings cases.  First Amendment and RLUIPA
challenges to land-use ordinances present the same problem Williamson County addressed in the takings context:
courts cannot determine if a regulation unlawfully interferes with a property use unti l it is reasonably clear how

27

the regulation applies.  RLUIPA’s text confirms that Congress contemplated that religious-liberty claims would be
subject to ordinary rules governing justiciability in the
land-use context.
C.  Petitioner’s challenges to the application of UHCO
§ 1274 are unripe.  The ordinance was never enforced
against petitioner.  And no credible threat of enforcement
existed because the Planning Commission never decided
how, or if, the ordinance appl ied to petitioner’s proposed
use.  Neither the cease-and-desist letter nor the Mayor’s
comments at the second Pl anning Commission hearing—
which both addressed use as a house of assembly—constituted credible threats of enforcement.
Petitioner’s attacks on the Sixth Circuit’s analysis are
unfounded.  He criticizes the court of appeals for failing to
address his “key” cases.  But petitioner cited almost none
of those cases to the Sixth Circ uit.  He also criticizes the
court of appeals for failing to  address his various claimed
injuries.  The Sixth Circuit, however, expressly addressed
his claimed First Amendment chill and found it insufficient, on this evidentiary record, to confer jurisdiction.
Pet.App.13a-14a.  Petitioner cites other supposed injuries,
but he did not explain below how these injuries are traceable to application of the ordinance and did not even
mention some of them at all.
III.  Applying Williamson County’s finality requirement to First Amendment and RLUIPA claims does not
burden religious liberty.
A.  The finality requirement does not apply to allegations that a land-use regulation infringes religious liberty
on its face.  Those claims ripe n as soon as the challenged
regulation is enacted.

28

B.  Because the finality re quirement is necessarily
context-specific, it will not apply to some religious-liberty
claims that do not turn on ap plication of a land-use regulation.  To the extent petitioner now tries to fit some of his
alleged injuries into this category, those arguments are

C.  When the finality requir ement does apply, it is a
relatively modest requirement.  Plaintiffs need only show
that ambiguities about the pe rmissible uses of property
have been resolved to a reason able degree of certainty.
And if a plaintiff can show th at proceedings before local
regulators would be futile, no further engagement with
the administrative process is required for a land-use claim

A. The Finality Requirement Determines When Challenges to Land-Use Regulations Are Unripe
“Under Article III, federal courts do not adjudicate
hypothetical or abstract disputes … [and] do not issue advisory opinions.”  TransUnion, 594 U.S. at 423-24.  Two

to ensure that cases present disputes that are “appropriately resolved through the judicial process.”  Trump v.
New York , 592 U.S. 125, 131 (2020) (citation omitted).
Standing requires plaintiffs to demonstrate they have suffered “an injury that is concrete, particularized, and
imminent rather than conjectural or hypothetical” that
arises from the defendant’s actions or, when challenging a
policy, “from the challenged policy itself.”  Id. at 131, 134
(citation omitted).  And ripe ness requires plaintiffs to
demonstrate that their claims do not depend on “contingent future events that may not occur as anticipated, or
indeed may not occur at all.”  Id. at 131 (citation omitted).
Standing and ripeness often “boil down to the same question,” SBA, 573 U.S. at 157 n.5, namely whether “judicial
resolution of th[e] dispute is premature,” New York, 592
U.S. at 134.
Justiciability doctrines like standing and ripeness are
grounded in separation-of-powers principles.  See FDA v.
All. for Hippocratic Med. , 602 U.S. 367, 378 (2024).  The

35

line between the lawful exercise of legislative and judicial
power often turns on “ when and at whose instance  [the
branches] are permitted to address” legal questions.  Antonin Scalia, The Doctrine of Standing as an Essential
Element of the Se paration of Powers , 17 Suffolk U. L.
Rev. 881, 892 (1983).  Courts must wait to decide legal
questions presented in “a concrete factual context.”  FDA,
602 U.S. at 379 (citation omitted ).  That means that “federal courts decide some co ntested legal questions later
rather than sooner,” while federal or local government actors consider those issues th rough the political process.
Id. at 380; see LGLC Amicus Br. 21.
In preenforcement lawsuits like this one, standing
and ripeness ensure that courts do not opine on the lawfulness of hypothetical govern ment action until plaintiffs
show a law will be enforced against them and how that law
will be applied.  California, 2026 WL 2473573, at *2.
Sometimes the justiciability in quiry is clear-cut.  But asapplied preenforcement challenges to land-use policies
are different.  Zoning codes comprise a web of general
rules and individualized exemptions.  Although zoning
codes outline how property generally may be used, provisions for special-use permits or variances supersede
general guidelines.  Thus, unlike challenged statutes that
facially compel or prohibit conduct, ordinarily a court cannot know whether a zoning ordinance as applied  to
specific property will limit an y particular use, or the extent of any limitations, until local authorities implement
the ordinance.  As the Uni ted States explains (at 16),
“[u]ntil authorities reach a fi nal decision, the contours of
local zoning requirements—and whether those requirements injure the plaintiff—will often be unclear.”

This Court has announced a rule specifying when
claims “challenging the application of land-use regulations” to specific property present justiciable, concrete
disputes in recognition of the flexible and discretionary
nature of land-use ordinances.  Palazzolo, 533 U.S. at 618,
620.  A claim challenging the application of a land-use regulation is not ripe until “a  land-use authority has the
opportunity, using its own reasonable procedures, to decide and explain the reach of a challenged regulation,”
such that the “permissible uses of the property are known
to a reasonable degr ee of certainty.”  Id. at 620.   This
rule—which the Court adopted in Williamson County Regional Planning Commission  v. Hamilton Bank of
Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)—has become known as
the “finality requirement.”  See Pakdel v. City & Cnty. of
San Francisco, 594 U.S. 474, 478 (2021).
The finality requirement ensures that zoning disputes
do not come to federal court prematurely, before there is
reasonable certainty that the challenged ordinance will do
what the plaintiff alleges it will.  When a plaintiff challenges the lawfulness of a land-use ordinance, this Court’s
cases “uniformly reflect an insistence on knowing the nature and extent of permit ted development before
adjudicating the constitutionality of the regulations that
purport to limit it.”  MacDonald, Sommer & Frates v.
Cnty. of Yolo, 477 U.S. 340, 351 (1986).  But finality does
not require exhaustion or “mul tiple layers of agency proceedings” before challenges to zoning ordinances are ripe.
Contra Pet. Br. 45, 50.  Finality requires only a “reasonable degree of certainty” abou t how the at-issue property
may be used under the challenged regulations.  Palazzolo,
533 U.S. at 620.
Most often, that certainty arises from land-use authorities (like planning commissions) actually applying the

zoning code—including any variance provisions—to the
at-issue property.  But a challenge to a zoning code may
also be ripe when there is “no question … about how the
regulations at issue apply to the particular land in question.”  Pakdel, 594 U.S. at 478 (citat ion omitted).  For
example, in Suitum v. Tahoe Regional Planning Agency,
the plaintiff could sue immediately because there was no
dispute that a regulation barred any “permanent land disturbance” on the plaintiff’s property and the land-use

her land.  520 U.S. 725, 739 (1997) (citation omitted).
B. The Finality Requirement Is Rooted in Article III
Williamson County’s finality requirement is an Article III rule.  Although petition er (at 39) claims it is “a
judge-made rule of ‘prudential ripeness,’”  the requirement from the start has been  grounded in Article III’s
case-or-controversy requirement, as the United States
agrees (at 15-17).  An as-applied challenge to a zoning ordinance does not present a concrete controversy—that is,
there exists no injury traceable to the ordinance’s application—without “a reasonable degree of certainty”
regarding whether and how the zoning ordinance applies
to the plaintiff’s desired land use.  Palazzolo, 533 U.S. at
620.  In cases like this one, the finality requirement is a
context-specific application of the ordinary rule that plaintiffs show a “credible threat of enforcement” to mount a
preenforcement challenge.  SBA, 573 U.S. at 161.
1.  Williamson County announced that the finality requirement addresses “whether  the initial decisionmaker
has arrived at a definitive position on the issue that inflicts
an actual, concrete injury .”  473 U.S. at 193 (emphasis
added).  That is indisputably Article III language.  See
Schlesinger v. Reservists Comm. to Stop the War, 418 U.S.
208, 220-21 (1974) (“Concrete injury, whether actual or

38

threatened, is that indispensable element of a dispute …
capable of judicial resolution.”); Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins ,
578 U.S. 330, 341 (2016) (“Arti cle III standing requires a
concrete injury.”).
This Court also has justified the finality requirement
in Article III terms both before and after Williamson
County.  Just a few years ago in Pakdel, this Court reaffirmed that the finality requirement “ensures that a
plaintiff has actually been injured by the Government’s action and is not prematurely suing over a hypothetical
harm.”  594 U.S. at 479 (citation omitted).  In Horne v. Department of Agriculture , the Court explained that “the
plaintiff’s takings claim in Williamson County failed because the plaintiff could not show that it had been injured
by the Government’s action” until the county applied the
zoning ordinance to the at-iss ue property.  569 U.S. 513,
525 (2013).  And in Agins v. City of Tiburon —on which
Williamson County relied, see 473 U.S. at 187—the Court
noted that because the plaint iffs “ha[d] not submitted a
plan for development,” there was “as yet no concrete controversy regarding the application of the specific zoning
provisions.”  447 U.S. 255, 260 (1980).
Williamson County aligns with this Court’s Article
III precedent addressing when plaintiffs have standing to
challenge laws.  Plaintiffs ch allenging laws may come to
court in two different ways.  They can “wait for the government to take coercive action” against them.  First
Choice Women’s Res. Ctrs., Inc. v. Davenport , 608 U.S.
174, 183 (2026).  Once the government takes action, the injury from the law is “actual” and “concrete,” and may be
remedied through either prospective or retroactive relief.
See id. ; Uzuegbunam v. Preczewski , 592 U.S. 279, 285
(2021) (retroactive relief possible when “officials enforced

39

[university’s] speech policies against [plaintiff]” (citations
omitted)).
Alternatively, plaintiffs “may bring a pre-enforcement suit seeking prospective relief against government
officials” if they “face[] ‘a credible threat of enforcement’”
that renders injury from the statute “concrete” and “imminent.”  First Choice, 608 U.S. at 183 (citing SBA, 573
U.S. at 161, 164-67).  A “credib le threat of enforcement”
requires plaintiffs to show th ey (1) intend to engage in
“conduct arguably affected with a constitutional interest,”
that (2) is “arguably proscribed by the statute they wish
to challenge,” where (3) the “threat of future enforcement
… is substantial.”  SBA, 573 U.S. at 161-64 (alterations
and citations omitted).
When plaintiffs bring a preenforcement challenge to
discretionary, fact-dependent zoning ordinances, Williamson County finality implements the requirement that
plaintiffs show a credible threat of enforcement.  The finality requirement recognizes that no credible threat
(and, therefore, no concrete injury) arises from application of zoning ordinances un til “the government entity
charged with implementing the regulations has reached a
final decision regarding the application of the regulations
to the property at issue.”  Williamson County, 473 U.S. at
186.  Put simply, plaintiffs ca nnot show that a proposed
use of their property is “arg uably proscribed by the statute they wish to challenge” until it is clear what the
ordinance proscribes.  See SBA, 573 U.S. at 162 (citation
and alteration omitted).
Because Williamson County pinpoints when land-use
regulations inflict concrete injuries, the finality requirement is not, as petitioner (a t 39) calls it, a “prudential”
relic.  This Court’s occasional reference to Williamson
County as a “prudential” decision is “a misnomer,” U.S.

40

described the requirement, 473 U.S. at 193.  “At its core,
Williamson County implements Article III.”  U.S. Br. 16.
And Article III itself serves prudential purposes.  As
the Sixth Circuit explained, finality “ensures that municipal land-use policy begins in local, politically accountable
hands.”  Pet.App.7a.  This is a core function of Article III,
which promotes the separation of powers by ensuring that
political decisions stay with political bodies.  See supra
p.34-35.  Finality, like other Article III doctrines, also promotes constitutional avoidance by ensuring that courts do
not decide constitutional questions when challenged laws

also Valley Forge Christian Coll. v. Americans United for

(1982) (Article III courts do not have “unconditioned authority to determine the consti tutionality of legislative or
executive acts,” but may do so as “a necessity in the determination of real, earnest and vital controversy” (citation

III. Williamson County ’s Finality Requirement Does Not
Threaten Religious Liberty
Petitioner (at 52-56) and his amici present a parade of
horribles that will supposedly follow if Williamson
County applies outside the takings context.  But the finality requirement will only bar claims for which no Article
III jurisdiction exists.  The requirement applies only to
claims, like petitioner’s, where the court cannot know if a
land-use regulation violates the plaintiff’s rights because
it is uncertain how a specific property can be used.  And
where the finality requirement  applies, it demands only
that a plaintiff wait to file su it until the government’s position is clear enough for the court to know that the
challenged regulation injures the plaintiff.

A. The Finality Requirement Does Not Apply to Facial
Challenges
Many religious-liberty claims are facial challenges to
laws, and the finality requirement does not apply to those
challenges.  See Yee v. City of Escondido, 503 U.S. 519, 534
(1992); Suitum, 520 U.S. at 736 & n.10.  A facial challenge
does not turn on how the government will ultimately apply
the regulation to a particular property.  See Pet.App.14a.
Notably, petitioner’s argument (at 25-26) that Williamson County  should not govern his as-applied
challenges relies heavily on First Amendment cases involving facial challenges.  Take City of Lakewood , which
petitioner (at 36) cites as an example of how “ordinary
rules” of standing apply “in the land-use context.”  Lakewood involved a facial preenforcement challenge to an
ordinance that gave a mayor unconstrained discretion to
issue permits for news racks on public land.  486 U.S. at
753-55.  Similarly, Watchtower Bible & Tract Society of
New York, Inc. v. Village of Stratton, 536 U.S. 150 (2002),
involved a facial preenforcement challenge to an ordinance prohibiting door-to-d oor canvassing without the
mayor’s prior approval.  Id. at 153.
In Freedman v. Maryland, 380 U.S. 51 (1965), the defendant facially challenged a film censorship statute after
he was criminally convicted for violating it.  Id. at 52-53,
56.  The case presented no ripeness question.  While Shuttlesworth v. City of Birmingham , 394 U.S. 147 (1969),
involved facial and as-applied challenges to an ordinance
requiring permits for public demonstrations, the defendant’s conviction likewise left no doubts about whether and
how the ordinance would apply to him.  See id. at 150-51,
156-58.

B. The Finality Requirement Applies Only to Claims

The finality requirement applies when a plaintiff challenges application of a land-u se regulation.  It does not
apply to other religious-liberty challenges to government

1.  Williamson County is not implicated when plaintiffs challenge action by gove rnment officers to restrict
land use apart from land-use regulations.  In those cases,
the court can evaluate the plaintiff’s claim without answering “how far” a land-use regulation goes.  Palazzolo, 533
U.S. at 622 (citation omitted).  For example, if rogue police
officers deter mosque attendance by threatening to arrest
worshippers who park on the street, that threat may inflict
a concrete injury immediately giving rise to a lawsuit.

C. The Finality Requirement Is Modest
In as-applied land-use challenges where Williamson
County’s finality requirement applies, finality is a “relatively modest” requirement.  Pakdel, 594 U.S. at 478.
Once the “potential ambiguities” about whether the imposition or implementation of a land-use regulation will
cause a plaintiff concrete harm have “evaporate[d],” the
claim will be ripe for review.  Id. at 479.
The finality requirement does not demand that plaintiffs pursue exceptions from local zoning authorities if
those efforts would be futile.  As the Sixth Circuit put it,
“‘futility’ is not an exception to finality; it’s another way to
state the rule.”  Pet.App.10a.  Futility can arise if the local
land-use authority has, as a practical matter, “dug in its
heels and made clear that [any] applications will be denied.”  Murphy, 402 F.3d at 349.  At that point, the
government has “committed to a position” and no further
engagement is necessary for the dispute to ripen.  Pakdel,
594 U.S. at 479.
Futility also occurs where regulators have “no discretion” over the permitted uses of a plaintiff’s land.  Suitum,
520 U.S. at 739.  Accordingly, the finality requirement will
not necessarily apply to gove rnment policies restricting
land use through means other than zoning ordinances.
See, e.g., Roman Catholic Diocese of Brooklyn v. Cuomo ,
592 U.S. 14, 15-16 (2020) (as-applied challenge to an emergency executive order limiting religious gatherings during
the COVID-19 pandemic).
Nor does finality require continued engagement with
pretextual or unduly dilatory administrative processes.
Contrary to petitioner’s claim (at 53) that Williamson
County allows regulators to “insulate their conduct from

57

review” by endlessly “postp on[ing] a final decision,” Williamson County  does not give government license to
“burden property by imposition  of repetitive or unfair
land-use procedures in order to avoid a final decision.”
Palazzolo, 533 U.S. at 621.
Petitioner’s land-use claims are unripe because he
sued before the ambiguity surrounding the ordinance’s
application to his gatherings had dissipated—not because
Williamson County set the bar for final ity too high.  The
Sixth Circuit properly rejected  petitioner’s futility argument because proceedings on petitioner’s permit
application “had not become an empty affair.”
Pet.App.11a.  And petitioner has never claimed that the
City imposed procedural requirements to avoid reaching
a final decision on his permit application.

Williamson County ’s finality requirement does not
empower municipalities to proh ibit prayer.  It enforces
Article III by preventing federal courts from prematurely
adjudicating disputes that ha ve yet to solidify into concrete cases.  This is one such case:  petitioner’s challenges
to the application of the Ci ty’s ordinance never crystallized into a concrete dispute.
